meta.titre: Radial and Transverse Acceleration: Components of motion in polar coordinates

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Further Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A camera operator stands on the quay at Bonanjo in Douala and follows a speedboat crossing the Wouri river. She never thinks in terms of east and north: she records how far the boat is from her and how far her camera has turned. Mechanics at Advanced Level often describes motion the same way, locating a particle by its distance from a fixed point and an angle. Paper 3 of the Cameroon GCE regularly asks you to turn that kind of information into speeds and accelerations, and it rewards candidates who know exactly which terms appear in each component.

items: Polar coordinates locate a point by its distance $r$ from the pole $O$ and an angle $\theta$, in radians, measured from the initial line.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
The chain rule gives $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\,\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$ and the product rule differentiates a product such as $r\dot\theta$.
A dot over a symbol means a derivative with respect to time $t$, so $\dot\theta$ is the angular speed in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

sections.titre: Velocity and acceleration in polar coordinates

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the particle stays at a fixed distance from $O$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Here $\dot r=\ddot r=0$, so $\mathbf v=r\dot\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ and $\mathbf a=-r\dot\theta^{2}\,\hat{\mathbf r}+r\ddot\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$. The radial part $-r\dot\theta^{2}=-v^{2}/r$ is the familiar acceleration towards the centre. The transverse part is present only when the angular speed is changing.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When $r$ is given as a function of $\theta$ and you need $\dot r$ and $\ddot r$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use the chain rule: $\dot r=f'(\theta)\,\dot\theta$. Differentiating again with the product rule gives $\ddot r=f''(\theta)\,\dot\theta^{2}+f'(\theta)\,\ddot\theta$. If $\dot\theta$ is constant then $\ddot\theta=0$ and only the first term of $\ddot r$ remains.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the only force on the particle is always directed towards, or away from, $O$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The force has no transverse component, so the transverse acceleration is zero. By (4), $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(r^{2}\dot\theta\right)=0$, hence $r^{2}\dot\theta=h$ is constant: it is the angular momentum per unit mass, in $\mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-1}}$. The transverse velocity is then $r\dot\theta=h/r$.

sections.contenu_markdown:
A particle $P$ moving in a plane is located by its polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ relative to a fixed pole $O$. Let $\hat{\mathbf r}$ be the unit vector along $OP$ (the **radial** direction, in which $r$ increases) and $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ the unit vector perpendicular to it in the sense of increasing $\theta$ (the **transverse** direction). As $\theta$ changes, both unit vectors turn:

$$\dot{\hat{\mathbf r}}=\dot\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta},\qquad \dot{\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}}=-\dot\theta\,\hat{\mathbf r}$$

Differentiating the position vector $\mathbf r=r\hat{\mathbf r}$ once and then twice gives the velocity and the acceleration:

$$
\mathbf v=\dot r\,\hat{\mathbf r}+r\dot\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\tag{1}
$$

$$
\mathbf a=\left(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}\right)\hat{\mathbf r}+\left(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta\right)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\tag{2}
$$

| Quantity | Radial component | Transverse component |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity | $\dot r$ | $r\dot\theta$ |
| Acceleration | $\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}$ | $r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$ |

The two directions are perpendicular, so the speed follows from Pythagoras' theorem:

$$
v^{2}=\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}\tag{3}
$$

The transverse acceleration can also be written in a compact form, which you can check by expanding with the product rule:

$$
r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=\frac{1}{r}\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(r^{2}\dot\theta\right)\tag{4}
$$

A negative radial component of acceleration points towards $O$. With $r$ in metres and $t$ in seconds, velocities are in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, accelerations in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $\dot\theta$ in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

etapes.justification: The formula for $r$ is a function of $\theta$ and $\theta=\pi/3$ is given.

etapes.action: Find $\dot r$ with the chain rule.
etapes.justification: The path gives $r$ in terms of $\theta$, so $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\dot\theta$.

etapes.action: Write down the velocity components and the speed.

etapes.justification: Differentiate $\dot r=-2\sin\theta\,\dot\theta$ again; since $\dot\theta$ is constant, $\ddot\theta=0$.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves in a plane so that, at all times, its polar coordinates satisfy $r=3+2\cos\theta$ (with $r$ in metres) and $\dot\theta=2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. When $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find

(a) the radial and transverse components of the velocity of $P$, and its speed,

(b) the radial and transverse components of the acceleration of $P$.
sections.conclusion_markdown: When $\theta=\pi/3$: the velocity has radial component $-2\sqrt3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and transverse component $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the speed is $2\sqrt{19}\approx 8.72\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The acceleration has radial component $-20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (towards $O$) and transverse component $-8\sqrt3\approx-13.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so its magnitude is $\sqrt{592}=4\sqrt{37}\approx24.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The radial component of acceleration is $\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}$, not $\ddot r$. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf r}$ keeps turning, so the velocity changes direction even when its size does not.
items.erreur_markdown: A particle moves on a circle of radius $2\ \mathrm{m}$ at the constant angular speed $3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. A student says: "$r$ is constant so $\ddot r=0$, hence the radial acceleration is zero."
items.correction_markdown: Radial acceleration $=0-2\times3^{2}=-18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, directed towards the centre.

items.pourquoi_faux: The transverse component is $r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. When $r$ is changing there is an extra term $2\dot r\dot\theta$ even if the angular speed is constant.
items.erreur_markdown: At an instant $r=4\ \mathrm{m}$, $\dot r=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\dot\theta=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ (constant). A student writes: transverse acceleration $=r\ddot\theta=0$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The radial and transverse components are perpendicular vectors, so they combine with Pythagoras' theorem, not by simple addition.
items.erreur_markdown: A student finds the speed from $\dot r=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $r\dot\theta=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ by writing $v=3+4=7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: $-2\sin\theta$ is $\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}$, a derivative with respect to the angle. The velocity component needs the derivative with respect to time.

items.enonce_markdown: A particle moves on a circle of radius $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ with centre $O$. At a certain instant its angular speed is $4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and is increasing at the rate of $6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$. Find, at that instant, the radial and transverse components of its acceleration and the magnitude of its acceleration.
items.solution_markdown:
On a circle, $\dot r=\ddot r=0$.

Radial component $=-r\dot\theta^{2}=-0.5\times4^{2}=$ **$-8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

Transverse component $=r\ddot\theta=0.5\times6=$ **$3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

Magnitude $=\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{73}\approx$ **$8.54\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves so that $r=(2\theta+1)$ metres and $\dot\theta=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ at all times. When $\theta=2$, find the radial and transverse components of the velocity, the speed, and the radial and transverse components of the acceleration of $P$.
items.solution_markdown:
When $\theta=2$: $r=2\times2+1=5\ \mathrm{m}$.

$\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\dot\theta=2\times3=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\ddot r=2\ddot\theta=0$ since $\dot\theta$ is constant.

Velocity: radial **$6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**, transverse $r\dot\theta=5\times3=$ **$15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**. Speed $=\sqrt{36+225}=\sqrt{261}=3\sqrt{29}\approx$ **$16.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

Acceleration: radial $=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}=0-5\times9=$ **$-45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**; transverse $=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=0+2\times6\times3=$ **$36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves in a plane under the action of a force which is always directed towards a fixed point $O$. At one instant $OP=4\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\dot\theta=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. At a later instant $OP=2\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\dot r=-7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(a) Explain why $r^{2}\dot\theta$ is constant and find its value.

(b) Find $\dot\theta$ at the later instant.

(c) Find the speed of $P$ at the later instant.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The force is directed towards $O$, so the transverse component of acceleration is zero: $\dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(r^{2}\dot\theta\right)=0$. Hence $r^{2}\dot\theta$ is constant, and at the first instant it equals $4^{2}\times3=$ **$48\ \mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-1}}$**.

(b) At the later instant $2^{2}\dot\theta=48$, so $\dot\theta=$ **$12\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$**.

(c) Transverse velocity $=r\dot\theta=2\times12=24\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Speed $=\sqrt{(-7)^{2}+24^{2}}=\sqrt{625}=$ **$25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

items_markdown: Velocity components: radial $\dot r$, transverse $r\dot\theta$; speed $v^{2}=\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}$.
If $r=f(\theta)$, use the chain rule: $\dot r=f'(\theta)\dot\theta$ and $\ddot r=f''(\theta)\dot\theta^{2}+f'(\theta)\ddot\theta$.
On a circle ($r$ constant) the radial acceleration is $-r\dot\theta^{2}$, towards the centre.
Under a central force the transverse acceleration is zero, so $r^{2}\dot\theta$ is constant.
